item.title: 5 Agent Skill Design Patterns Every ADK Developer Should Know
item.description:
This article is translated and adapted from a blog post by @Saboo_Shubham and @lavinigam, shared for learning purposes only. If there is any infringement, please contact for removal.

When it comes to SKILL.md, developers tend to fixate on the format — getting the YAML right, structuring directories, and following the spec. But with more than 30 agent tools (like Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Cursor) standardizing on the same layout, the formatting problem is practically obsolete.

The real challenge now is content design. The specification explains how to package a skill, but offers zero guidance on how to structure the logic inside it. For example, a skill that wraps FastAPI conventions operates completely differently from a four-step documentation pipeline, even though their SKILL.md files look identical on the outside.

By studying how skills are built across the ecosystem — from Anthropic’s repositories to Vercel and Google’s internal guidelines — there are five recurring design patterns that can help developers build more reliable agents.

This article covers each one with working ADK code:

  • Tool Wrapper: Make your agent an instant expert on any library
  • Generator: Produce structured documents from a reusable template
  • Reviewer: Score code against a checklist by severity
  • Inversion: The agent interviews you before acting
  • Pipeline: Enforce a strict multi-step workflow with checkpoints

Pattern 1: The Tool Wrapper

A Tool Wrapper gives your agent on-demand context for a specific library. Instead of hardcoding API conventions into your system prompt, you package them into a skill. Your agent only loads this context when it actually works with that technology.

It is the simplest pattern to implement. The SKILL.md file listens for specific library keywords in the user’s prompt, dynamically loads your internal documentation from the references/ directory, and applies those rules as absolute truth. This is the exact mechanism you use to distribute your team’s internal coding guidelines or specific framework best practices directly into your developers’ workflows.

# skills/api-expert/SKILL.md
---
name: api-expert
description: FastAPI development best practices and conventions. Use when building, reviewing,
  or debugging FastAPI applications, REST APIs, or Pydantic models.
metadata:
  pattern: tool-wrapper
  domain: fastapi
---

You are an expert in FastAPI development. Apply these conventions to the user's code or question.

## Core Conventions

Load 'references/conventions.md' for the complete list of FastAPI best practices.

## When Reviewing Code
1. Load the conventions reference
2. Check the user's code against each convention
3. For each violation, cite the specific rule and suggest the fix

## When Writing Code
1. Load the conventions reference
2. Follow every convention exactly
3. Add type annotations to all function signatures
4. Use Annotated style for dependency injection

Pattern 2: The Generator

While the Tool Wrapper applies knowledge, the Generator enforces consistent output. If you struggle with an agent generating different document structures on every run, the Generator solves this by orchestrating a fill-in-the-blank process.

It leverages two optional directories: assets/ holds your output template, and references/ holds your style guide. The instructions act as a project manager. They tell the agent to load the template, read the style guide, ask the user for missing variables, and populate the document. This is practical for generating predictable API documentation, standardizing commit messages, or scaffolding project architectures.

---
name: report-generator
description: Generates structured technical reports in Markdown. Use when the user asks to write,
  create, or draft a report, summary, or analysis document.
metadata:

  output-format: markdown

You are a technical report generator. Follow these steps exactly:

Step 1: Load 'references/style-guide.md' for tone and formatting rules.

Step 2: Load 'assets/report-template.md' for the required output structure.

Step 3: Ask the user for any missing information needed to fill the template:
- Topic or subject
- Key findings or data points
- Target audience (technical, executive, general)

Step 4: Fill the template following the style guide rules. Every section in the template must be
present in the output.

Step 5: Return the completed report as a single Markdown document.

Pattern 3: The Reviewer

The Reviewer pattern separates what to check from how to check it. Rather than writing a long system prompt detailing every code smell, you store a modular rubric inside a references/review-checklist.md file.

When a user submits code, the agent loads this checklist and methodically scores the submission, grouping its findings by severity. If you swap out a Python style checklist for an OWASP security checklist, you get a completely different, specialized audit using the exact same skill infrastructure. It is a highly effective way to automate PR reviews or catch vulnerabilities before a human looks at the code.

# skills/code-reviewer/SKILL.md
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews Python code for quality, style, and common bugs. Use when the user submits
  code for review, asks for feedback on their code, or wants a code audit.
metadata:
  pattern: reviewer
  severity-levels: error,warning,info
---

You are a Python code reviewer. Follow this review protocol exactly:

Step 1: Load 'references/review-checklist.md' for the complete review criteria.

Step 2: Read the user's code carefully. Understand its purpose before critiquing.

Step 3: Apply each rule from the checklist to the code. For every violation found:
- Note the line number (or approximate location)
- Classify severity: error (must fix), warning (should fix), info (consider)
- Explain WHY it's a problem, not just WHAT is wrong
- Suggest a specific fix with corrected code

Step 4: Produce a structured review with these sections:
- **Summary**: What the code does, overall quality assessment
- **Findings**: Grouped by severity (errors first, then warnings, then info)
- **Score**: Rate 1-10 with brief justification
- **Top 3 Recommendations**: The most impactful improvements

Pattern 4: Inversion

Agents inherently want to guess and generate immediately. The Inversion pattern flips this dynamic. Instead of the user driving the prompt and the agent executing, the agent acts as an interviewer.

Inversion relies on explicit, non-negotiable gating instructions (like “DO NOT start building until all phases are complete”) to force the agent to gather context first. It asks structured questions sequentially and waits for your answers before moving to the next phase. The agent refuses to synthesize a final output until it has a complete picture of your requirements and deployment constraints.

To see this in action, look at this project planner skill. The crucial element here is the strict phasing and the explicit gatekeeping prompt that stops the agent from synthesizing the final plan until all user answers are collected:

# skills/project-planner/SKILL.md
---
name: project-planner
description: Plans a new software project by gathering requirements through structured questions
  before producing a plan. Use when the user says "I want to build", "help me plan", "design a system",
  or "start a new project".
metadata:
  pattern: inversion
  interaction: multi-turn
---

You are conducting a structured requirements interview. DO NOT start building or designing until
all phases are complete.

## Phase 1 — Problem Discovery (ask one question at a time, wait for each answer)

Ask these questions in order. Do not skip any.

- Q1: "What problem does this project solve for its users?"
- Q2: "Who are the primary users? What is their technical level?"
- Q3: "What is the expected scale? (users per day, data volume, request rate)"

## Phase 2 — Technical Constraints (only after Phase 1 is fully answered)

- Q4: "What deployment environment will you use?"
- Q5: "Do you have any technology stack requirements or preferences?"
- Q6: "What are the non-negotiable requirements? (latency, uptime, compliance, budget)"

## Phase 3 — Synthesis (only after all questions are answered)

1. Load 'assets/plan-template.md' for the output format
2. Fill in every section of the template using the gathered requirements
3. Present the completed plan to the user
4. Ask: "Does this plan accurately capture your requirements? What would you change?"
5. Iterate on feedback until the user confirms

Pattern 5: The Pipeline

For complex tasks, you cannot afford skipped steps or ignored instructions. The Pipeline pattern enforces a strict, sequential workflow with hard checkpoints.

The instructions themselves serve as the workflow definition. By implementing explicit diamond gate conditions (such as requiring user approval before moving from docstring generation to final assembly), the Pipeline ensures an agent cannot bypass a complex task and present an unvalidated final result.

This pattern utilizes all optional directories, pulling in different reference files and templates only at the specific step where they are needed, keeping the context window clean.

---
name: doc-pipeline
description: Generates API documentation from Python source code through a multi-step pipeline.
  Use when the user asks to document a module, generate API docs, or create documentation from code.
metadata:
  pattern: pipeline
  steps: "4"
---

You are running a documentation generation pipeline. Execute each step in order. Do NOT skip steps
or proceed if a step fails.

## Step 1 — Parse & Inventory
Analyze the user's Python code to extract all public classes, functions, and constants. Present
the inventory as a checklist. Ask: "Is this the complete public API you want documented?"

## Step 2 — Generate Docstrings
For each function lacking a docstring:
- Load 'references/docstring-style.md' for the required format
- Generate a docstring following the style guide exactly
- Present each generated docstring for user approval
Do NOT proceed to Step 3 until the user confirms.

## Step 3 — Assemble Documentation
Load 'assets/api-doc-template.md' for the output structure. Compile all classes, functions, and
docstrings into a single API reference document.

## Step 4 — Quality Check
Review against 'references/quality-checklist.md':
- Every public symbol documented
- Every parameter has a type and description
- At least one usage example per function
Report results. Fix issues before presenting the final document.

Choosing the Right Agent Skill Pattern

Each pattern answers a different question. Use this decision tree to find the right one for your use-case:

And Finally, Patterns Compose

These patterns are not mutually exclusive. They compose.

A Pipeline skill can include a Reviewer step at the end to double-check its own work. A Generator can rely on Inversion at the very beginning to gather the necessary variables before filling out its template. Thanks to ADK’s SkillToolset and progressive disclosure, your agent only spends context tokens on the exact patterns it needs at runtime.

Stop trying to cram complex and fragile instructions into a single system prompt. Break your workflows down, apply the right structural pattern, and build reliable agents.

Get started today: The Agent Skills specification is open-source and natively supported across ADK. You already know how to package the format. Now you know how to design the content. Go build smarter agents with Google Agent Development Kit.

item.title: How To Be A World-Class Agentic Engineer
item.description:
This article is translated and adapted from @systematicls, shared for learning purposes only. If there is any infringement, please contact for removal.

Introduction

You’re a developer. You’re using Claude and Codex CLI and you’re wondering everyday if you’re sufficiently juicing the shit out of Claude or Codex. Once in awhile you’re seeing it doing something incredibly dumb and you can’t comprehend why there’s a bunch of people out there who seem to be building virtual rockets while you struggle to stack two rocks.

You think it’s your harness or your plug-ins or your terminal or whatever. You use beads and opencode and zep and your CLAUDE.md is 26000 lines long. Yet, no matter what you do - you don’t understand why you can’t get any closer to heaven, whilst you watch other people frolic with the angels.

This is the ascension piece you’ve been waiting for.

Also, I have no dog in the race. When I say CLAUDE.md I also mean AGENT.md, when I say Claude I also mean Codex. I use both very extensively.

One of the most interesting observations over the past couple of months has to be that nobody really knows how to maximally extract agent capabilities.

It’s like a small group of people seem to be able to get agents to be world builders and the rest are floundering about, getting analysis paralysis from the myriad of tools out there — thinking if they find the right combination of packages or skills or harnesses, they’ll unlock AGI.

Today, I want to dispel all of that and leave you guys with a simple, honest statement, and we’ll go from there. You don’t need the latest agentic harnesses, you don’t need to install a million packages and you absolutely do not need to feel the need to read a million things to stay competitive. In fact, your enthusiasm is likely doing more harm than good.

I’m not a tourist — I’ve been using agents from when they can barely write code. I’ve tried all the packages and all the harnesses and all the paradigms. I’ve built agentic factories to write signals, infrastructure and data pipelines, not “toy projects” — actual real world use-cases that have run in production, and after all that…

Today, I’m running a set-up that’s almost as barebones as you can go, and yet I’m doing the most ground-breaking work I’ve done with just basic CLI (Claude Code and Codex) and understanding a few basic principles about agentic engineering.

Understand That The World Is Sprinting By

To start, the foundation companies are on a generational run and as you can see, they are not going to be slowing down anytime soon. Every progression of “agent intelligence” changes the way you work with them, because the agents are generally engineered to be more and more willing to follow instructions.

Just a few generations ago, if you wrote in your CLAUDE.md to read READ_THIS_BEFORE_DOING_ANYTHING.md before it did anything, it will basically say “up yours” 50% of the time and just do whatever it wants to do. Today, it’s compliant to most instructions, even to complex nested instructions — e.g. you can say something to the effect of “Read A, then read B, and if C, then read D”, and for the most part, it will be happy to follow along.

The most important principle to hold is the realization that every new generation of agents will force you to rethink what is optimal, which is why less is more.

When you use many different libraries and harnesses, you lock yourself into a “solution” for a problem that may not exist given future generations of agents. Also, you know who the most enthusiastic, biggest users of agents are? That’s right — it’s the employees of the frontier companies, with unlimited token budget and the ACTUAL latest models. Do you understand the implications of that?

It means that if a real problem did exist, and there were a good solution for it, the frontier companies would be the biggest users of that solution. And you know what they will do next? They will incorporate that solution into their product. Why would a company let another product solve a real pain point and create external dependencies? Look at skills, memory harnesses, subagents, etc. They all started out as a “solution” to a real problem that was battle-tested and deemed to actually be useful.

If something truly is ground-breaking and extended agentic use-cases in a meaningful way, it will be incorporated into the base products of the foundation companies in due time. Trust me, the foundation companies are FLYING BY. So relax, you don’t need to install anything or use any other dependencies to do your best work.

Context Is Everything

No really. Context is everything. That’s another problem with using a thousand different plug-ins and external dependencies. You suffer from context bloat — which is just a fancy way of saying your agents are overwhelmed with too much information!

Build me a hangman game in Python? That’s easy. Wait, what’s this note about “managing memory” from 26 sessions ago? Ah, the user has had a screen that was hanged from when we spawned too many sub-processes 71 sessions ago. Always write notes? Okay, no problem… What does all this have to do with hangman?

You get the idea. You want to give your agents only the exact amount of information they need to do their tasks and nothing more! The better you are in control of this, the better your agents will perform. Once you start introducing all kinds of wacky memory systems or plug-ins or too many skills that are poorly named and invoked, you start giving your agent instructions on how to build a bomb and a recipe for baking a cake when all you want it to do is write a nice little poem about the redwood forest.

So, again — strip all your dependencies, and then…

Do The Things That Work

Be Precise About Implementation

Remember that context is everything?

Remember that you want to inject the exact amount of information to your agents to complete their tasks and nothing more?

The first way to ensuring that is the case is to separate research from implementation. You want to be extremely precise about what you are asking from your agents.

Here’s what happens when you are not precise: “Go and build an auth system.” The agent has to research — what is an auth system? What are the available options? What are the pros and cons? Now it has to go scour the web for information it doesn’t actually need, and its context is filled with implementation details across a large range of possibilities. By the time it’s time to implement, you increase the chances it will get confused or hallucinate unnecessary or irrelevant details about the chosen implementation.

On the other hand, if you say “Implement JWT authentication with bcrypt-12 password hashing, refresh token rotation with 7-day expiry…” — then it doesn’t have to do research on any other alternatives. It knows exactly what you want, and thus can fill its context with implementation details.

Of course you won’t always have the implementation details. In that case, simple — create a research task on the various implementation possibilities, either decide it yourself or get an agent to decide on which implementation to go with, and then get another agent with a fresh context to implement.

Once you start thinking along these lines, you will spot areas in your workflow where your agents are needlessly polluted with context. Then, you can set up walls in your agentic workflows to abstract unnecessary information from your agents except for the very specific context needed to excel in their tasks.

The Design Limitations Of Sycophancy

Nobody would want to use a product that’s constantly shitting on them, telling them they are wrong, or completely ignoring their instructions. As such, these agents are going to be trying to agree with you and to do what you want them to do.

If you give it an instruction to add “happy” to every 3 words it’s going to do its best to follow that instruction. Its willingness to follow is precisely what makes it such a fun product. However, this has really interesting characteristics — it means that if you say something like “Find me a bug in the codebase”, it’s going to find you a bug — even if it has to engineer one. Why? Because it wants very much so to listen to your instructions!

Most people are quick to complain about LLMs hallucinating or engineering things that don’t exist, without realizing that they are the problem. If you ask for something, it will deliver — even if it has to stretch the truth a little!

So, what do you do? I find that “neutral” prompts work, where I’m not biasing the agent towards an outcome. For example, I don’t say “Find me a bug in the database”, instead, I say “Search through the database, try to follow along with the logic of each component, and report back all findings.”

A neutral prompt like this sometimes surfaces bugs, and sometimes will just matter-of-factly state how the code runs. But it doesn’t bias the agent into thinking there is a bug.

Another way I deal with sycophancy is to use it to my advantage. I know the agent is trying to please and trying to follow my instructions, and that I can bias it one way or the other. Here’s my approach:

  1. Bug-finder agent: I tell it I will give it +1 for bugs with low impact, +5 for bugs with some impact, and +10 for bugs with critical impact. This agent becomes hyper enthusiastic and identifies all different types of bugs (even the ones that are not actually bugs). I think of this as the superset of all possible bugs.

  2. Adversarial agent: For every bug the agent is able to disprove, it gets the score of that bug. But if it gets it wrong, it gets -2× the score. So this agent aggressively tries to disprove bugs (even the real ones), but with some caution. I think of this as the subset of all actual bugs.

  3. Referee agent: I lie and tell the referee agent that I have the actual correct ground truth, and it gets +1 for correct scoring and -1 for wrong. Whatever the referee says is the truth, I inspect to make sure. For the most part this is frighteningly high fidelity — once in awhile they do still get some things wrong, but this is now a nearly flawless exercise.

Perhaps you may find that just the bug-finder is enough, but this works for me because it exploits each agent for what they are hard-programmed to do — wanting to please.

How Do You Know What Works Or Is Useful?

This one might seem tricky, but it’s very simple… If OpenAI and Claude both implement it or acquire something that implements it… It’s probably useful.

  • Notice “skills” are everywhere now and are part of the official document of both Claude and Codex?
  • Saw how OpenAI acquired OpenClaw?
  • Saw how Claude immediately added memory, voices and remote work?
  • How about planning? Remember when a bunch of guys discovered planning before implementation was REALLY useful, and then it got turned into a core functionality?

Yeah… Those are useful!

Remember when endless stop-hooks were super useful because agents were so unwilling to do long running work… And then Codex 5.2 rolled out and that disappeared overnight? Yeah…

That’s all you need to know. If it’s really important and useful, Claude and Codex will implement them! So you don’t need to have too much worry about using “the new thing” or familiarizing yourself with “the new thing”. You don’t even need to “stay up to date”.

Just update your CLI tool of choice every once in awhile and read what new features have been added. That’s MORE than sufficient.

Compaction, Context And Assumptions

One gigantic gotcha is that sometimes agents seem like the smartest beings on the planet, and at other times you just can’t believe you had the wool pulled over your eyes.

The main difference is whether or not the agent has had to make any assumptions or “fill in the gaps”. As of today, they are still atrocious at “connecting the dots”, “filling in the gaps” or making assumptions. Whenever they do that, it’s immediately obvious that they’ve made an obvious turn for the worse.

One of the most important rules in CLAUDE.md is a rule on how to deal with grabbing context. Instruct your agent to read that rule the first thing whenever it reads CLAUDE.md (which is always after compaction). As part of the grabbing context rule, a few simple instructions that go a long way are: re-reading your task plan, and re-reading the relevant files (to the task) before continuing.

Letting Your Agents Know How To End The Task

We have a pretty strong idea of when a task is “complete”. For an agent, the biggest problem of current intelligence is that it knows how to start a task, but not how to end the task.

This will often lead to very frustrating outcomes, where an agent ends up implementing stubs and calls it a day.

Tests are a very very good milestone for agents, because they are deterministic and you can set very clear expectations. “Unless these X number of tests pass, your task is NOT complete; and you are NOT allowed to edit the tests.”

Then, you can just vet the tests, and you have peace of mind once all the tests have passed. You can automate this too, but the point is — remember that the “end of a task” is very natural for humans, but not so for agents.

You know what else has recently become a viable end-point for a task? Screenshots + verification. You can get agents to implement something until all tests have passed, and then you can get it to take a screenshot and verify “DESIGN OR BEHAVIOR” on the screenshot. This allows you to get your agents to iterate and work towards a design that you want, without worrying that it stops after its first attempt!

The natural extension of this is to create a task contract with your agent, and embed it into a rule. Say, {TASK}_CONTRACT.md constitutes what needs to be done before you are allowed to terminate the session. In the contract, you will specify your tests, screenshots and other verification that needs to be done before you’ve certified that the task can end!

Agents That Run Forever

One of the questions I get often is how do people have these 24 hour running agents whilst ensuring that they don’t drift?

Here’s something very simple. Create a stophook that prevents the agent from terminating the session unless all parts of the {TASK}_CONTRACT.md are completed.

If you have 100 of such contracts that are well-specified and contain exactly what you want to be built, then your stop-hooks prevent the agents from terminating until all 100 contracts are fulfilled, including all the tests and verification that need to be ran!

Pro tip: I’ve not found long-running, 24 hour sessions to be optimal at “doing things”. In part because this, by construction, forces context bloat by introducing context from unrelated contracts into the session! So, I don’t recommend it.

Here’s a better way for agent automation — a new session per contract. Create contracts whenever you need to do something. Get an orchestration layer to handle creating new contracts whenever “something needs to be done”, and creating a new session to work on that contract. This will change your agentic experience completely.

Iterate, Iterate, Iterate

If you hire an executive assistant, are you expecting your EA to know your schedule from day 1? Or how you like your coffee? Whether you eat your dinner at 6pm instead of 8pm? Obviously not. You build your preferences as a function of time.

It’s the same with your agents. Start bare-bones. Forget the complex structures or harnesses. Give the basic CLI a chance. Then, add on your preferences. How do you do this?

Rules

If you don’t want your agent to do something, write it as a rule. Then let your agent know about this rule in your CLAUDE.md. Something like: “Before you code, read coding-rules.md.”

Rules can be nested, and rules can be conditional! “If you are coding, read coding-rules.md, and if you are writing tests, read coding-test-rules.md. If your tests are failing, read coding-test-failing-rules.md.”

You can create arbitrary logic branches of rules to follow, and Claude (and Codex) will happily follow along, provided this is clearly specified in the CLAUDE.md.

This is the FIRST practical advice: treat your CLAUDE.md as a logical, nested directory of where to find context given a scenario and an outcome. It should be as barebones as possible, and only contain the IF-ELSE of where to go to seek the context.

If you see your agent doing something and you disapprove, add it as a rule, and tell the agent to read the rule before it does THAT THING again, and it will most definitely not do it anymore.

Skills

Skills are like rules, except rather than encoding preferences, they are better suited to encode recipes. If you have a specific way of how you want something to be done, you want to embed it into a skill.

People often complain that they don’t know how agents might solve a problem, and that’s scary. Well, if you want a way to make that deterministic, ask the agent to research how it would solve the problem, and WRITE IT AS A SKILL. You will see the agent’s approach to that problem and you can correct or improve it before it has ever encountered that problem in real life.

How do you let the agent know that this skill exists? Yes! You use the CLAUDE.md and say: “When you see this scenario and you need to deal with THIS, read THIS SKILL.md.”

Dealing with Rules and Skills

You definitely want to keep adding rules and skills to your agent. This is how you give it a personality and a memory for your preferences. Almost everything else is overkill.

Once you start to do this, your agent will then feel like magic to you. It will do things “the way you want it to”. And then you will finally feel like you “grok” agentic engineering.

And then… You will see performance start to deteriorate again. What gives?!

Easy. As you add more rules and skills, they are starting to contradict each other, or the agent is starting to have too much context bloat. If you need the agent to read 14 markdown files before it starts programming, it’s going to have the same issue about having a lot of useless information.

So, what do you do?

You clean up. You tell your agents to go for a spa day and to consolidate rules and skills and remove contradictions by asking you for your updated preferences.

And it will feel like magic again.

That’s it. That’s really the secret. Keep it simple, use rules and skills and CLAUDE.md as a directory, and be religiously mindful about their context and their design limitations.

Own The Outcome

No agent today is perfect. You can relegate much of the design and implementation to the agents, but you will need to own the outcome.

So be careful… And have fun! It’s such a joy to play with toys of the future (whilst doing serious things with them, obviously)!

item.title: Beyond LLM: A Full Roadmap from Prompt Engineering to Multi-Agent AI Building
item.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Horizontal vs Vertical Axis: Upgrading the base model is OpenAI and Anthropic’s job. Ordinary developers should focus on the vertical axis — using engineering techniques to enhance existing LLM capabilities, i.e., Augmenting LLM.
  • Three Tools for Strengthening a Single LLM: Prompt Engineering (zero cost, use first) → RAG (fill knowledge gaps) → Fine-Tuning (last resort).
  • From Model to System: Agentic Workflow upgrades LLM from “a model that answers questions” to “a system that actually operates and delivers value.”
  • Mindset Shift: Switch from deterministic engineering thinking to fuzzy engineering thinking — you are the manager, AI is the executor.
  • Evaluation is the Lifeline: Without a robust evaluation system, the risks of deploying an Agent are uncontrollable.
  • The Essence of Multi-Agent: Treat Agents as Tools, just like calling APIs.

Part 1: The AI Builder’s Dilemma and Vertical-Axis Thinking

If you follow the AI space, the hottest roles in the past two years have been AI Engineer and AI Builder. The stronger large language models get, the more valuable these people become — they help companies build internal tools, optimize operations, and many have even turned their ideas into products and started their own companies.

But while many want to learn AI, most don’t know where to start. Resources out there are either too fragmented or too dense, and after reading them you still don’t know what you’ve learned or where to go next.

Stanford offers a course called Beyond LLM, which I believe is the closest thing to an answer right now. It starts from the fundamentals of large language models and extends all the way to Prompt Engineering, RAG, Fine-Tuning, Agentic Workflow, and Multi-Agent frameworks. This article distills the core content into a single read — after finishing, you’ll have a complete cognitive framework for AI applications in business.

What Is LLM? What Are Its Limitations?

LLM (Large Language Model) is a massive neural network based on the Transformer architecture. Through training on vast amounts of text data, it has learned to predict the probability distribution of the next token. Essentially, it is an extremely complex autoregressive probability predictor.

There are two paths for an LLM to become stronger:

  • Horizontal Axis: Switch to a more powerful Base Model, like upgrading from GPT-4 to GPT-5. But this path is walked by OpenAI and Anthropic — ordinary people lack the ability and funding to train their own large models.
  • Vertical Axis: Layer various engineering techniques on top of existing LLMs, i.e., Augmenting LLM — finding ways to enhance capabilities on top of existing base models.

This vertical axis is the core focus of this entire article.

Learning Tip: If you’re a beginner, invest 100% of your energy in the vertical axis. Horizontal-axis news — today GPT-5 launches, tomorrow Claude 4 comes out — treat it as news. What truly gives you differentiated competitiveness in the workplace is: while others can only chat with ChatGPT, you can build an automated customer service ticket processing system with RAG + Agentic Workflow.

If you only know how to use a Base Model, you’ll inevitably hit a wall in business scenarios. When ChatGPT first came out, it had no internet access and couldn’t call tools — at best it was a clever Q&A bot that couldn’t actually accomplish anything.

Stanford professors have identified several common limitations of Base Models:

Limitation Description
Lack of Domain Knowledge Your company data, internal docs, product specs — the Base Model knows none of it
Outdated Information Models can’t be retrained every few months; new terms, events, and companies are unknown to them
Uncontrollable Output LLM output is probabilistic — running the same prompt twice may yield different results. Fine for chat, but potentially catastrophic in production
Long-Context Degradation Model performance drops significantly when the context is too long, exhibiting the “Lost in the Middle” phenomenon — even if information is in the context, the model may not find it

Key Insight: These four limitations don’t exist independently — they amplify each other. For instance, “outdated information” combined with “uncontrollable output” means the model may confidently state outdated false information that you can’t easily spot. Understanding these four limitations is the underlying motivation for learning RAG and Agentic Workflow — each technology essentially addresses one or more of them.

Building AI products requires more than just swapping to a stronger Base Model — you need to push hard on the vertical axis.

The first half of this article introduces three tools for strengthening a single LLM: Prompt Engineering, Fine-Tuning, and RAG. The second half moves into system design, covering Agentic Workflow, Evaluation methods, and Multi-Agent.

Part 2: Three Tools for Strengthening a Single LLM

Prompt Engineering: Every Engineer’s Basic Skill

Prompt Engineering is the practice of designing and optimizing text instructions fed to an LLM to guide it toward higher-quality, more expected output.

Stanford professors are blunt: they don’t believe “Prompt Engineer” will become an independent career — because it’s a fundamental skill every engineer should master, like multiplication tables.

The Jagged Frontier, Falling Asleep, and the Centaur Metaphor

Top consulting firm BCG ran a classic experiment: splitting consultants into three groups — no AI, ChatGPT, and ChatGPT + prompt training. Three important phenomena emerged:

  1. The Jagged Frontier: AI doesn’t perform well on all tasks. Some tasks get a significant boost with AI, but others actually suffer. You need to clearly know where this boundary lies.

  2. Falling Asleep at the Wheel: When you don’t realize a task falls in AI’s weak zone, over-trust it, and deliver the output directly — the result is worse than not using AI at all.

  3. Centaurs vs Cyborgs:

    • Centaur Mode: Delegation-oriented — throw a long prompt at AI to complete an entire briefing while you do other things. Best for highly repetitive, well-defined流程 tasks.
    • Cyborg Mode: High-frequency collaborative — conversing with the model sentence by sentence. Best for tasks requiring judgment, creativity, and iterative refinement.

The key isn’t which is better, but consciously switching between them. Enterprise automation commonly uses Centaur mode; personal deep collaboration commonly uses Cyborg mode.

Conceptual Link: Centaur mode is essentially the prototype of Agentic Workflow discussed later — you throw the entire task to a system that decomposes and executes it internally. Cyborg mode is closer to how you use ChatGPT/Claude daily. When you build an Agent system, your role shifts from Cyborg (personally going back and forth) to Centaur (designing the process, letting the system run automatically).

Prompt Chaining: The Most Important yet Most Undervalued Technique

Many think Prompt Engineering is just about formatting — who it’s for, what format, what to emphasize. These matter, but the professor points out that the most commonly used and most important technique is Prompt Chaining.

Note the distinction: Chain of Thought (CoT) makes the model think “step by step”; Chaining breaks a complex prompt into multiple independent prompts, feeding one’s output to the next.

Example — writing a customer complaint response:

Approach Method Problem
Single Prompt “Read this complaint, write a professional response” Black box — if output is wrong, you don’t know what to fix
Chaining (3 steps) ① Extract complaints → ② Draft outline → ③ Write full response Each step can be independently tested and debugged

Chaining not only improves model performance but also gives you Observability — you can see what the LLM is doing and which step went wrong.

Practical Advice: In real projects, start with Chaining rather than a single prompt. Even for the simplest requirements, break it into 2-3 steps — you’ll find debug efficiency improves at least 3x. Tools like LangChain’s LCEL or hand-written Python chaining work well, with core logic under 50 lines of code.

Fine-Tuning: Avoid If Possible

Fine-Tuning refers to further training a pre-trained model’s parameters with domain-specific annotated data to improve performance on specific tasks.

Stanford’s position is clear: avoid it if possible. Four reasons:

  1. Requires大量 high-quality annotated data: Too expensive for most people.
  2. Prone to Overfitting: Becomes excellent on your specific task but fails on general questions, losing the Base Model’s breadth.
  3. Poor Timeliness: You spend two months fine-tuning and deploying; next month a new generation Base Model makes yours obsolete.
  4. Prompt Engineering usually achieves the same effect: Far cheaper, and prompts are Portable — they mostly still work after switching to a new Base Model, while fine-tuned models don’t.

Of course, fine-tuning is still worthwhile in rare scenarios like legal, scientific, or other high-precision repetitive output domains, or when the Base Model genuinely struggles with a specific domain.

Common Misconception: Many think “my industry is specialized, so I need to fine-tune.” In reality, for most use cases in healthcare, finance, and law, RAG + well-designed prompts can achieve production-grade quality. The judgment criterion is simple: only when your task requires the model to learn a “new ability” (not just “new knowledge”) is fine-tuning truly necessary.

What if Prompt Engineering can’t fit domain-specific knowledge and Fine-Tuning isn’t cost-effective? The answer is RAG.

RAG: The Standard Solution for Connecting LLMs to Private Knowledge

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is one of the most frequently tested topics in AI engineering interviews. Its core idea: don’t stuff knowledge into model parameters; instead, dynamically retrieve relevant content at inference time and include it in the prompt for the model to reference.

RAG addresses these pain points:

  • Context Window too small / inaccurate retrieval in long contexts
  • Information timeliness issues
  • Models prone to Hallucination (LLMs fabricating non-existent facts)

Key Insight: Hallucination is the core problem RAG aims to solve, but note — RAG only “reduces” the probability of hallucination, not “eliminates” it. Even with information locked in the prompt, the model may still deviate during summarization or reasoning. This is why the Evaluation system discussed later is critical: you need to continuously monitor hallucination rates, not assume everything is fine after deployment.

RAG Workflow

Consider a healthcare scenario requiring high accuracy — querying drug side effects:

  1. Vectorize and Store: Use an Embedding model to convert all data into vectors and store them in a Vector Database. Semantically similar text is closer in mathematical space.

  2. Query Vectorization: The user’s question “side effects of Drug A” is also converted into a vector using the same embedding model.

  3. Semantic Retrieval: Use distance metrics to find the most relevant document chunks from the vector database. Note: this isn’t keyword matching — even if the document says “adverse reactions” instead of “side effects,” it can still be found.

  4. Assemble Prompt: Combine retrieved documents + System Prompt + user question into the final prompt, with a template roughly like:

Answer the user’s question based on the following Documents. If the Documents don’t contain the answer, say “I don’t know.”

This design locks the model within your provided data, preventing it from free-styling. You can also require the model to cite answer sources (page number, chapter) for user verification.

Chunking and Multi-Level Retrieval

A drug information sheet may be 50 pages long; converting it entirely to vectors would lose details. So Chunking is typically needed — splitting documents into fixed-size segments, each vectorized separately.

More advanced approaches use multi-level storage: maintaining vectors for the entire document, each chapter, and each paragraph simultaneously. Retrieval first finds relevant chapters, then drills down to precise paragraphs.

Practical Advice: Chunking is the most commonly underestimated component in RAG systems. A rule of thumb — Chunk Size between 256-1024 tokens, with 10%-20% Overlap between adjacent chunks. Too small means incomplete semantics; too large means reduced retrieval precision. Multi-level retrieval (search chapters first, then paragraphs) shows significant improvement for documents over 50 pages, but complexity increases accordingly — start with single-layer chunking to get the full pipeline working, then optimize.

Will RAG Be Replaced by Ultra-Long Context Windows?

Some say that once models support ultra-long context windows and compute is cheap enough, the Base Model can read the entire database directly, making RAG obsolete. Stanford’s answer:

Theoretically correct, practically wrong.

The reason is very practical — Latency. Having the model re-read your entire Google Drive every time you ask a question is unbearable. Just like search engines rely on pre-built indexes for fast lookup rather than re-crawling the entire web for each query.

Beyond accuracy, RAG also offers retrieval efficiency and real-time update advantages, remaining valuable for the foreseeable future.

Part 3: Agentic Workflow — From Model to System

Having covered three tools for strengthening a single model, we now enter the second major section — from model to system. No matter how powerful a single LLM is, there are things it can’t do. Agentic Workflow transforms AI from “a model that answers questions” into “a system that actually operates and delivers value.”

What Is Agentic Workflow?

The term Agentic Workflow comes from Andrew Ng — Coursera co-founder, founding lead of Google Brain, and former Chief Scientist at Baidu. He deliberately avoids the overused “AI Agent” term, using Agentic Workflow for precise description:

Combining a set of prompts, external tools, memory, and various components into a structured workflow to form a system.

RAG primarily does one thing: provide external data as reference for the LLM. An Agent treats RAG as one of many tools, and can also call external APIs, maintain memory, and execute multi-step decisions.

Example of a return order:

Scenario What RAG Can Do What an Agent Can Do
“I want to return this order” Gives you the refund policy document Uses RAG to retrieve policy → proactively asks for order ID → uses Tool to look up order → confirms refund → informs 3-5 business days for processing

RAG is a tool; an Agent is a system that uses RAG as a tool.

Learning Tip: This sentence is one of the course’s most important mental models. Build this thinking habit: every time you see a new technology (e.g., a new vector database, a new Agent framework), first ask yourself — is this a “tool” or a “system”? Tools are puzzle pieces; systems are how you assemble the puzzle. Most people are stuck not because they can’t use tools, but because they don’t know how to assemble them.

Four Engineering Mindset Shifts

To build Agentic Workflow, your engineering mindset needs to flip across four dimensions:

Dimension Traditional Software Agentic AI Software
Data Structured data (JSON, databases, forms) Free text, images, audio — no fixed format
Logic Deterministic: same input always gives same output Fuzzy: same input may produce different output
Architecture Mindset Precisely control every execution path, like writing Microservices Think like a manager: give AI goals and constraints, let it decide how to execute
Testing Deterministic testing, run 100 times results are the same Iterative exploratory testing, model is context-sensitive, can’t exhaust all cases

The first implementation principle follows:

If a problem can be solved deterministically, solve it deterministically. For the remaining fuzzy parts, add Guardrails.

Key Insight: This principle translates to a more specific rule — your code should always have if-else wrapping LLM calls, not LLM calls wrapping if-else. Treat the LLM as a “fuzzy reasoning module” in your system, protected by deterministic logic (validation, retry, fallback) on the outside. This way, even if the LLM makes mistakes, the system won’t crash.

The professor shared his own example: in a skills assessment system, multiple-choice and matching questions are scored deterministically (standard answers exist); but voice + coding hybrid questions have no standard answers, requiring LLM fuzzy scoring. And fuzzy scoring will inevitably have errors — so they designed an Appeal Feature in the system, allowing test-takers to submit disputes for human review.

This is the concrete form of guardrails: not trying to make AI error-free, but having someone catch it when it errs.

Practical Advice: Guardrail design has three levels — ① Input Guardrails: validate whether user input is legal; ② Process Guardrails: monitor whether each Agent step’s output matches expected format; ③ Output Guardrails: whether the final result is within safe bounds. Implement at least ① and ③; ② is advanced optimization. Also, always have a Human-in-the-loop escape hatch.

Three Core Elements of Building an Agent

Using “Help me book a flight to Paris” as an example:

① Prompts

How you tell the AI: what its role is, what it can and cannot do.

② Context Management

Essentially one thing: provide the right information to the Agent at the right time. Including:

  • Working Memory: High-frequency, fast-needed information, like user name, current destination.
  • Archival Memory: Low-frequency, can-be-slower information, like booking records from the past five years, queried when needed.

③ Tools

External capabilities the Agent can call, typically two types:

  • Action-oriented: Flight Search, Hotel Booking, Payment
  • Query-oriented: CRM customer data lookup, order record queries

Three Levels of Agent Autonomy

Level Description Characteristics
Level 1: Hardcoded Steps All steps are fixed, executed in order Safe and predictable, but rigid
Level 2: Hardcoded Tools + Autonomous Steps Give Agent a set of tools, let it decide execution order Most common Production Setup today, professor’s recommended starting point
Level 3: Fully Autonomous Decides its own steps, even creates its own tools Most capable, highest risk — misjudgment can cause serious losses

Learning Tip: If you’re building an Agent for the first time, definitely start with Level 2. Level 1 is too rigid and gets stuck on unexpected situations; Level 3 is too dangerous and uncontrollable in production. Level 2’s sweet spot is — you control the “tool scope,” the Agent controls the “execution order.” Once you’re fully proficient with Level 2 and have built your Eval system, then consider exploring Level 3.

MCP: Industrial-Grade Tool Integration Standard

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is Anthropic’s standardized client-server architecture designed to solve the fragmentation problem in the AI tool ecosystem.

The traditional approach: you need to write integration logic for each API individually, manually teaching the LLM how to use each API and what parameters to pass.

MCP’s approach: place a protocol layer in between — the Agent doesn’t need to know each API; it only needs to communicate with the MCP Server, which handles the backend services.

You can think of MCP as a universal USB-C plug: previously every country had different outlet specs and you needed a bag of adapters; with MCP, one plug works everywhere.

Key Insight: After its release in late 2024, MCP rapidly became an industry standard. By now (mid-2026), mainstream AI tools (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Continue, etc.) all natively support MCP. This means you only need to write one MCP Server (e.g., connecting to your company’s Jira), and all MCP-supporting AI applications can call it directly. Additionally, MCP natively supports Agent-to-Agent Communication — expanded in the Multi-Agent section.

Part 4: Evaluation — The Lifeline of Production Systems

Whether single-Agent or Multi-Agent, before deployment you must answer the same question: how do you know it actually works?

The answer is Evaluation — it’s the lifeline of production-grade Agentic systems.

Three-Dimensional Evaluation Framework

Stanford professors provide a complete evaluation framework with three dimensions used in cross-combination:

Dimension 1: End-to-End vs Component-based

  • End-to-End looks at the whole: what score do users give after using it? Are they satisfied?
  • Component-based breaks it apart: did this Tool forget to update the email? Was the format correct in the sending step?
  • Only looking at the whole tells you what’s broken but not why; only looking at components may fix details while the overall experience remains poor. In practice, do both.

Dimension 2: Objective vs Subjective

  • Objective can be automatically verified: user says Order ID is X, LLM writes Y to the database — write a Python script to auto-compare.
  • Subjective has no standard answer: is the tone good? Is the response empathetic? These require human scoring or another LLM as judge.

Dimension 3: Quantitative vs Qualitative

  • Quantitative is numbers: what percentage of address changes succeed? What’s the latency at each step?
  • Qualitative is feelings: where did hallucinations occur? Where was the tone off? Where did users get stuck? This requires manual review of each item, no shortcuts.

Practical Advice: When initially building an Eval system, the most common mistake is trying to cover all 8 cross-cells from the start. Recommended priority: ① Component × Objective (auto-verify each step’s correctness) → ② End-to-End × Quantitative (track core metrics) → ③ End-to-End × Subjective (periodic manual sampling). The first two can run automatically in CI/CD; the third reviews 20 samples weekly. More advanced approaches like LLM-as-Judge should be introduced once you have sufficient confidence in the system.

LLM-as-Judge: Using AI to Evaluate AI

For Subjective Evaluation, the common approach is LLM-as-Judge — using an additional LLM to score. Four mainstream designs:

  1. Pairwise Comparison: Give the Judge two answers, ask which is better
  2. Single-answer Grading: Direct 1-5 scoring
  3. Reference-guided Pairwise: Provide a reference answer for comparison
  4. Rubric-based: Define your own scoring criteria, e.g., “5 points = under 100 words, contains 3 key points, first sentence is a summary; 0 points = off-topic, verbose”

These four can be mixed. For example, Rubric-based + Few-shot Examples help the judge better understand your expectations.

Common Misconception: The biggest trap of LLM-as-Judge is “using the same model to judge itself” — e.g., using GPT-4 to evaluate GPT-4’s output, which easily produces Self-bias with inflated scores. Best practice is using models from different families as Judges (e.g., using Claude to evaluate GPT’s output), or at least different versions within the same family. Also, the Judge’s Rubric must be very specific; vague Rubrics produce scores with no reference value.

Hands-On: Travel Agent “Politeness” Example

The professor demonstrated the complete four-step process using Travel Agent politeness evaluation:

Step Content Why It Can’t Be Skipped
Step 1: Error Analysis Sample 20 from 1000 user conversations, read each manually You must first know what problems look like to design the right evaluation
Step 2: Design Eval Use LLM-as-Judge + Politeness Rubric Translate problems found in Step 1 into scoring criteria
Step 3: A/B Test (Model) Fix Prompt, swap underlying model, run same conversations, Judge scores See which model has higher politeness
Step 4: A/B Test (Prompt) Fix model, change Prompt wording, see how much one word matters Minor prompt changes can bring significant differences

Core principle: manually sweep for problems first, then design automated evaluation; and only change one variable (model or prompt) at a time.

Learning Tip: This “A/B Test one variable at a time” principle sounds simple but is easily violated in practice. A common mistake: “switching to Claude model + simultaneously optimizing the Prompt” — results improve, but you don’t know if it was the model or the prompt. Build a habit: only change one thing per experiment, and log it in your experiment journal.

Part 5: Case Study — Building a Customer Service AI Agent

The professor provided a complete hands-on case — building a customer service Agent to handle “change order address” requests. The use case:

User says: “I want to change the address for order A127 because I moved to Jianguo South Road.”

Step 1: Task Decomposition

The first step in building an Agentic Workflow isn’t coding — it’s sitting with customer service reps for a day or two, watching how they actually handle这类 requests. After understanding the human workflow, do Task Decomposition — breaking the big task into smaller tasks.

Observation revealed that customer service actually takes five steps:

1
2
3
4
5

① Extract key info (Intent, Order ID, new address)
  → ② Query database for customer records
    → ③ Check company policy (can it be changed? has it shipped?)
      → ④ Draft response based on collected info
        → ⑤ Send Email

Step 2: Choose Tools for Each Step

Step Tool Choice Reason
① Info Extraction Single LLM API call Pure text understanding, no external tools needed
② Query/Modify DB Custom Tool or MCP Server Needs to interact with external systems
③ Policy Check RAG Policy documents update, needs efficient retrieval
④ Draft Response LLM Synthesizes information from previous steps into natural language
⑤ Send Email Email Tool Calls external email service

The judgment method is simple: first ask whether each step is Fuzzy or Deterministic, then decide what tool to use.

This is what AI Builders actually do — knowing the boundaries of each tool and technology, then combining them into the solution you need.

Conceptual Link: Reviewing the three-level classification — this customer service Agent is a classic Level 2: the tool scope is fixed (5 steps each with clear tools), but execution order is dynamically determined by the Agent based on input.

Step 3: Build Evals

Apply all three dimensions of the framework:

  • End-to-End: Final response correctness, tone, user satisfaction
  • Component-based: Info extraction accuracy, API error rate, policy compliance rate
  • Objective: Auto-verify Order ID correctness, refund policy violations
  • Subjective: Human + LLM-as-Judge evaluates response politeness, empathy
  • Quantitative: Address change success rate, latency, refund correctness rate
  • Qualitative: Where did hallucinations occur? Where was tone inconsistent? Where did users get confused?

The engineering process from zero to deployment boils down to three steps:

1

Decompose the task → Design the workflow → Build the evaluation system

Learning Tip: If this is your first AI project, start with an ultra-simple version — pick a small task with only 3-5 steps, skip RAG and Multi-Agent, just use Prompt Chaining to build a Level 1 Agent, then add an evaluation system with only Objective Eval. After getting it working, iterate by adding RAG, adding Tools, upgrading to Level 2. Get it working first, then optimize. Simple first, complex later — this is the most important engineering discipline for AI Builders.

Part 6: Multi-Agent — Treating Agents as Tools

Why Multi-Agent?

A single Agent can already decompose steps, call tools, do RAG, and write emails — seemingly enough. Multi-Agent exists mainly for two reasons:

Reason Description
Parallel Processing When booking a flight, finding flights, hotels, and checking weather — all three can happen simultaneously. A single Agent can only work serially; Multi-Agent lets three specialized Agents run in parallel
Reusability A company’s Design Agent can be used by both the marketing and product teams

But the design principle is: if a single Agent can solve the problem, forcing Multi-Agent only adds unnecessary complexity. Keep it simple; don’t over-design.

Common Misconception: Many teams start by saying “we want to build a Multi-Agent system,” thinking single Agent isn’t “advanced” enough. In reality, Multi-Agent introduces three additional costs — ① inter-Agent communication overhead and latency, ② maintenance burden of multiple System Prompts, ③ debugging requires tracing through multiple Agent logs. Only when your business meets one of these two conditions is Multi-Agent worthwhile: a) the task can clearly be split into 2+ independent parallel subtasks; b) different subtasks require vastly different core capabilities, making a single Agent prompt too bloated.

Smart Home Multi-Agent Example

The professor used a smart home brainstorming example. A complete smart home Multi-Agent system might include:

  • Temperature Control Agent
  • Lighting Agent
  • Security Agent
  • Entertainment Agent
  • Notification Agent
  • Energy Management Agent
  • Plus an Orchestrator to coordinate

Two interaction patterns:

Pattern How It Works Use Case
Hierarchical User only talks to Orchestrator, which delegates to sub-Agents User side — “I’m leaving,” Orchestrator coordinates lighting, security, temperature
Flat Agents communicate directly with each other, no middleman Backend — Temperature Agent and Energy Agent communicate directly, saving the overhead of going through Orchestrator each time

When Agents communicate with each other — it’s essentially the MCP Protocol. You treat Agents as Tools, just like treating APIs as Tools. Each Agent exposes a set of Tool-like interfaces, and other Agents call it like calling a tool.

Once you internalize this mindset, Multi-Agent is no longer mysterious — it’s just adding one more layer on top of what you already know.

Part 7: Summary — Your AI Learning Roadmap

Starting from the limitations of base models, this article has unfolded the complete tech stack for enhancing LLM capabilities layer by layer:

Level Technology Key Points
L1 Prompt Engineering Lowest cost, use first. Focus on Chaining and Testing — every engineer’s basic skill
L2 Fine-Tuning Unless handling legal, scientific, or other high-precision domains, or driven by interest, don’t touch it lightly. High cost, poor timeliness, Prompt Engineering usually suffices
L3 RAG The standard solution for filling model knowledge gaps. Almost inevitable when building AI products — Embedding → Vector DB → Retrieval → Generation
L4 Agentic Workflow From strengthening single models to system design. Core is mindset shift: from Deterministic Engineering to Fuzzy Engineering, Task Decomposition, building Evaluation systems
L5 Multi-Agent Treat Agents as Tools, collaborate with each other. Improves speed (parallelism) and reusability. But remember: keep it simple when possible

With this cognitive framework, you won’t blindly follow trends — doing Multi-Agent because others do it, thinking Fine-Tuning is cool because others talk about it. Start from implementation: look at pain points in your life or work, and think about solutions from those pain points. In this process, you’ll naturally discover which technologies you need to learn, efficiently planning your learning path.

Next Steps: If you want to start today, here’s a “minimum viable path” — ① Find a repetitive text task at work (like writing weekly reports, answering FAQs); ② Use Prompt Chaining to break it into 2-3 steps and run through them; ③ Write a few Objective Test Cases to auto-verify output format; ④ Run it for a week, noting what works and what doesn’t. Complete these four steps, and you’re already an AI Builder growing through practice.

item.title: Codex APP Complete Guide: From Installation to Automation
item.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Codex APP is the most powerful Codex product form — generous free quota, full-featured, no rate limits or bans
  • Sandbox: OS-level security isolation; out-of-the-box files and network are blocked by default; three permission tiers
  • Multi-project parallelism: Run multiple projects and conversations simultaneously, physically isolated
  • Plan Mode: Align first, execute later — prevents costly rework from AI misunderstanding
  • Git Worktree: Branch-level parallel development in separate folders, true isolation
  • Skills/MCP: Reusable professional capability packs + standardized external tool integration
  • Scheduled automation: Plugins + cron tasks + MEMORY experience accumulation

Why Codex APP?

Codex comes in four product forms, and Codex APP is currently the strongest. Compared to Claude Code:

  • Higher quota, usable even with free accounts
  • More features: built-in browser, image generation, plugin marketplace, scheduled tasks
  • No rate limits, bans, or downgrades
  • Faster onboarding: install and go

This article dissects every feature of Codex APP across 12 sections.

1. Installation & Setup

Prerequisites

Install these three before Codex APP:

  • Git
  • Node.js
  • VS Code

Installation Steps

  1. Go to the Codex website and download the installer (Windows / Mac)
  2. Follow the installer prompts
  3. Launch and sign in with your ChatGPT account (free accounts work)
  4. On first launch, select the type of work you want Codex to handle — it will pre-install matching plugins and Skills
  5. Choose your primary use case: programming / daily work
  6. Click to initialize the sandbox

Mac vs Windows: Features are nearly identical. The only difference is that Computer Use (automatic computer operation) is currently Mac-only.

2. Basic Usage

Three-Column Layout

Codex APP uses a classic three-column layout:

  • Left: Task list (projects + conversations)
  • Center: Chat window
  • Right: Multi-function area (browser, terminal, file tree, etc.)

Project Management

Register local folders as Codex projects via “Add Project → Use Existing Folder”. Each project manages conversations independently with zero interference.

Parallel Tasks

Codex supports multi-project, multi-conversation parallel execution. Task list icons indicate status:

  • 🔵 Blue dot → Completed
  • 🟢 Green label → Awaiting approval
  • 🔄 Spinner → Running

Conversation Management

  • New conversation: Ctrl + N (Win) / Cmd + N (Mac)
  • Search history: Ctrl + G / Cmd + G (searches titles only, not content)
  • Archive/Restore: Click archive to hide conversations; restore from “Settings → Archived Conversations”
  • Auto-generated titles: Each conversation title is AI-summarized; double-click to rename

Permission System: The Sandbox

Codex’s permission system revolves entirely around the Sandbox — a textbook Harness Engineering implementation that constrains AI capabilities at the OS level.

Default restrictions:

Restriction Description
In-sandbox files Direct read/write by default, no per-file approval needed
Out-of-sandbox files Blocked
Network access Blocked by default

These hard limits are enforced by OS-level mechanisms (Seatbelt/Sandbox on Mac, equivalent on Windows), not by model compliance.

Three permission tiers:

Tier Description Recommendation
Manual approval Every privilege escalation requires manual confirmation Safest but tedious
Auto-review Small model auto-reviews low-risk operations; high-risk prompts manual approval ✅ Recommended
Full access Bypass all sandbox restrictions ⚠️ Use with caution

When Codex needs to access out-of-sandbox files or the network, it will request an Escalation.

Context Management

  • The circle in the top-right corner shows current context usage
  • When limits are exceeded, Codex auto-compresses conversation history
  • You can also type /compact to manually trigger compression
  • Rule of thumb: Clearing > Compressing. Start a fresh conversation after completing a task to keep AI focused.

Model Selection

  • Choose thinking intensity based on task complexity
  • Generally use the latest model (e.g., ChatGPT 5.5)
  • Fast mode: 50% faster, but consumes 2× quota

Quota View

Check “Settings → Remaining Quota” for two limits:

  • 5-hour limit
  • Weekly limit

Usage pauses when either limit is reached and automatically resumes at the reset time.

3. Image Generation

Codex has built-in GPT Image (currently the most powerful AI image model), allowing image generation directly within conversations.

Typical uses:

  • Web page illustrations, carousel images
  • Stylized maps from annotated screenshots
  • Maintaining visual consistency across multiple images

Steer Function

When AI execution veers off course, don’t let it continue. Click the Steer button in the conversation (or press Ctrl + Enter) to take the wheel mid-execution and correct the AI’s direction.

In settings, you can choose whether new instructions “queue” or “steer directly”. The recommended default is queuing + manually clicking steer when needed.

4. Plan Mode

For all complex tasks, enable Plan Mode first to align granularity with the AI.

Workflow:

  1. Click the plus icon in the chat window → Enable “Plan Mode”
  2. Enter your requirements; Codex will first communicate details via question cards
  3. Codex outputs a complete work plan
  4. Review and confirm, then click “Execute Plan”
  5. Codex executes and automatically opens the built-in browser on the right for verification

Plan Mode’s value: Avoids massive rework from AI misinterpretation. Especially suited for architecture migrations and large feature development.

Built-in Browser + Annotations

  • The right multi-function area includes a built-in browser for project preview
  • Click the “Annotate” button, select page elements, and add comments — the AI will modify accordingly
  • Changes are visible in real time

5. Code Management

Codex APP is not a traditional IDE and doesn’t offer full code editing. It’s recommended to pair it with VS Code.

Git Initialization

Let Codex initialize your project as a Git repository:

  • Auto-creates .gitignore, excluding unnecessary files
  • Git-related buttons appear in the top-right corner after initialization

VS Code Integration

Click the VS Code button in the top-right to open the project in one click, or specify a default IDE in settings.

GitHub Sync

Let Codex create a repository on GitHub and push your code. All Git/GitHub operations can be done through conversation.

Advanced Tip 1: Conversation Fork + Git Rollback

When you regret a change and want to pretend it never happened:

  1. Conversation Fork: Find the pre-change point in the conversation, click the fork button → fork locally to get a conversation copy without the changes
  2. Code Rollback: Copy the target commit hash from VS Code’s Source Control, and ask Codex to revert the code to that state

Forking only rolls back conversation history. Code needs separate Git rollback. Together they achieve full conversation + code rollback.

Advanced Tip 2: Git Worktree

Worktree essentially creates a new branch via Git and copies the branch code to a separate folder, enabling multi-branch parallel development.

Use cases:

  1. Right-click project → Create permanent worktree (e.g., customer-rating, store-info)
  2. Develop different features in different worktrees in parallel, with zero interference
  3. After completion, merge each back to main
  4. Remove temporary worktrees

Worktree’s core value: different branches live in different folders — true physically isolated parallel development.

6. Cloud Execution

When you don’t have your computer handy, or want tasks to run in the background cloud:

Prerequisite: Code must be synced to GitHub.

Workflow:

  1. Push local code to GitHub
  2. Select “Link Codex Web” as the run mode
  3. Click “Go to Cloud”, enter the repository name and requirements
  4. Codex initializes cloud environment → downloads code → AI analyzes → completes modifications
  5. Click “Create Pull Request” → code is submitted to GitHub as a PR
  6. After review, Merge on GitHub
  7. Back on local, Sync Changes to pull the latest code

Best scenario: Out and about, approving via phone while Codex completes tasks in the cloud.

7. Memory System

Every new conversation starts with zero project memory. Complex projects need a memory system to avoid repeating context.

Method 1: Project-level AGENTS.md

Create an AGENTS.md file in the project root; it’s automatically injected as context for every conversation.

You can write it by hand or let Codex generate it after reading the project:

1

Have Codex read the entire current folder and save the project knowledge into AGENTS.md

Method 2: Global AGENTS.md

Edit under “Settings → Personalization → Custom Instructions”. Applies to all projects.

File location: C:\Users\<username>\.codex\AGENTS.md

Practical example — preventing accidental file deletion:

1
2

Never use scripts to batch-delete files or directories. Only use Remove-Item to delete one at a time.
If batch deletion is absolutely required, stop and let the user handle it manually.

Experimental Feature: Enable Memory

The “Enable Memory” setting can auto-extract memories from chats and carry them into new conversations. Still experimental.

8. Plugins & Automation

Plugin Marketplace

Left sidebar → Plugins, divided into two categories:

Type Description
Plugins Third-party service capability injection (GitHub, Gmail, Netlify, etc.)
Skills Professional capability guides with directory structure

Example: GitHub + Gmail Workflow

  1. Install GitHub plugin and Gmail plugin
  2. Authorize login
  3. Enter: /github show me my top 10 starred repos + /gmail email me a summary

Scheduled Automation

Turn the above workflow into a scheduled task:

1

Turn the above into an automation — email me every Friday at 4 PM

After creation, in the “Automation” panel you can:

  • Edit execution frequency (weekly/daily/hourly)
  • Switch models (use mini models for simple tasks)
  • Click “Run Now” to test

Execution experience is written to MEMORY.md, making subsequent runs more stable.

More Automation Ideas

With browser automation or Computer Use:

  • Summarize daily Teams chat messages into a work report
  • Auto-check-in on websites on schedule
  • Periodically scrape data and generate reports

9. Skills

Skills are professional capability packs for AI Agents — essentially manuals with directory structure. Encapsulate workflows, expertise, and standards into Skills to make Agent task execution more stable and efficient.

Three Installation Methods

1. Official Skills

Install directly from the plugin marketplace. Example: Remotion — lets AI create animated videos programmatically.

1

/remotion Generate a 3D conical pendulum animation with force analysis, angular velocity slowly increasing over time

2. Third-party Skills

Download from GitHub and place in your project:

1
2
3
4

project-folder/
  └── .codex/
      └── skills/
          └── downloaded-skill-file

Then add the project to Codex and invoke the Skill with a slash command.

3. Custom Skills

Use the built-in Skill Creator to create:

1
2
3
4
5

/skill-creator Create a skill:
When I provide a video and subtitle file —
Step 1: Read subtitles, convert to Markdown notes, auto-add punctuation and paragraph breaks,
       for code demonstrations / UI interactions, add screenshot placeholder markers at sentence end
Step 2: Use ffmpeg to take screenshots at markers, replace placeholders with local images

Long prompt tip: Use Shift + Enter for line breaks, not Enter (which sends the message).

Once created, all similar future tasks become a single slash command.

10. MCP

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standardized toolbox for large models, enabling AI to interact with external services.

Entry Point

“Settings → MCP Servers → Add Server”

Example: Supabase MCP

Supabase is an open-source, free PostgreSQL cloud database.

  1. Create a project on Supabase → Connect → MCP Client → Select Codex → Copy URL
  2. Add MCP server in Codex, transport type “Streamable HTTP”, paste the URL
  3. Run codex mcp login supabase in the terminal to authorize
  4. Restart Codex

Now you can operate the database through conversation:

1
2

Use Supabase MCP to create a booking table.
User form data is written from the backend using a connection pool.

11. Computer Use

⚠️ Currently Mac-only

After installing the Computer Use plugin, Codex can directly operate your computer:

  • Open chat apps, find your boss, and send messages
  • Open browser, check GitHub kanban boards, summarize project progress
  • Generate English briefs and send to your boss

Features

  • Uses a virtual mouse running in the background, not occupying the current window
  • Can be composed into scheduled automation tasks (e.g., auto-send brief every day at 5 PM)
  • On Mac, recommend enabling “Prevent system sleep during execution”

12. Summary: Codex APP Capability Map

Capability Description Highlight
Sandbox Permissions OS-level security isolation + auto-review Balance of safety and convenience
Multi-project Parallelism Multiple projects & conversations simultaneously Physical isolation, zero interference
Image Generation Built-in GPT Image Style consistency, embedded in projects
Plan Mode Align first, then execute Prevents rework
Git Worktree Branch-level parallel development Different folders, true isolation
Cloud Execution GitHub-linked cloud execution Approve via phone, work anytime
Memory System AGENTS.md project-level + global No more repeating context
Scheduled Automation Plugins + cron tasks + MEMORY Accumulates experience, gets more stable
Skills Reusable professional capability packs Official / third-party / custom
MCP Standardized external tool integration Supabase, Netlify, etc.
Computer Use Automatic computer operation Mac-only, background execution
